as_told: Test pilot Bob Hoover was flying home from an air show when both engines of his plane quit; a young mechanic had filled it with jet fuel instead of gasoline. Hoover got the plane down. Instead of shouting at the crying mechanic, he put his arm around him and said he wanted him to service his plane the next day, and in some versions made him his only mechanic.
lesson: Forgiving a person's mistake and showing trust in them, instead of criticising, makes them do better.
what_happened: In his autobiography 'Forever Flying' (1996), Hoover writes that after an air show performance he told the line boy who drove the fuel truck to service his Aero Commander Shrike quickly. The Shrike was fuelled with jet fuel; Hoover writes that he and his passengers then 'climbed up the ravine' and were taken back to Brown Field, so the aircraft came down off the airfield. He quotes a Fullerton (Calif.) News-Tribune article of the next day: he found the boy in tears, put his arm around him and said he wanted him to be 'the only one to refuel my plane tomorrow'. The 1981 Carnegie retelling, citing the magazine Flight Operations, calls the aircraft a 'World War II propeller plane' and has Hoover say 'service my F-51 tomorrow'.

lesson_verdict.why: I found no study that tests this specific claim. I could not search for one because the session's web-search budget was used up.

search_steps: Read the English Wikipedia article 'Bob Hoover' as a lead. It says a jet-fuel accident happened to his Shrike Commander and cites Forever Flying pp. 275-277; it does not mention the line boy.

Open Library search-inside for "service my F-51": 25 hits, all in Carnegie editions or later books that copy it. The earliest reliably dated one is the 1981 Simon and Schuster revised edition (howtowinfriendsi0000carn). Hits dated 1948 and 1964 are combined editions whose metadata dates are probably wrong, because the passage appears to have been added in the 1981 revision; I did not check the 1936 text.

Open Library search-inside for "Bob Hoover, a famous test pilot" and "World War II propeller plane" Hoover: the same Carnegie passage, and later books that name the magazine Flight Operations as Carnegie's source.
The 1981 Carnegie edition and Forever Flying (foreverflyingfif00hoov, foreverflying00rabo) are lending-only. archive.org refused the full-text download (HTTP 401) and the in-book search (HTTP 403).

Found Hoover's passage with Open Library search-inside for "line boy" Shrike, then read it forward by repeated phrase searches, each starting from the last words of the previous snippet (about 20 queries, 31 s apart). Each response is saved as JSON, with a plain-text extract that removes the highlight marks.
Fetched the FAA Safety Briefing of July-August 2005 cited by Wikipedia on misfuelling. It does not mention Hoover, so it was not kept.

Could not read the Fullerton News-Tribune article Hoover cites, nor the Flight Operations article Carnegie cites. Did not search Google Books, HathiTrust or newspaper archives because the session's web-search budget was used up.
confidence_note: All quotes come from Open Library search snippets, not from a full text, but the snippets join into one continuous passage of Hoover's own words. Hoover's account is a 1996 retelling that quotes a newspaper report of the next day, which I did not see. I could not fix the date of the accident or whether anyone was hurt; Wikipedia, a lead only, says Hoover was seriously injured. The common version gets the aircraft wrong (a Shrike Commander, not a Second World War fighter) and turns 'the only one to refuel my plane tomorrow' into 'his only mechanic'. The lesson does not depend on these details, so the class is 'true'.
